one_line: Eugene Yan (Anthropic) walks through a six-step harness for using LLMs to find, verify, triage and patch vulnerabilities, arguing the bottleneck has moved from finding bugs to verification, triage and patching.
summary: Eugene Yan, a member of technical staff at Anthropic, argues that finding vulnerabilities with frontier models is now easy, so the bottleneck has shifted to verification, triage and patching. He describes a six-step loop: write a threat model and build an isolated sandbox as setup, then run discovery, verification, triage and patching. The key design choice is splitting discovery (optimised for recall) from an independent, adversarial verifier (optimised for precision) that sees only the claimed vulnerability and confirms it with a proof of concept in a fresh container. He stresses that context (threat models, compensating controls, business severity) matters more than prompt cleverness, and that closing the loop by turning each fix into a regression check makes the harness compound over time. He ends with organisational bottlenecks (routing, severity calibration, patch review) and advice to start interactively on open-source dependencies. Most numbers come from Mozilla's public bug-fix counts and one open-source scan, and the talk is mostly a practitioner process rather than a product pitch.

key_ideas.idea: Finding vulnerabilities is now straightforward; the bottleneck has moved to verification, triage, patching and organisational process.
key_ideas.detail: Speaker cites Mozilla's monthly security fixes: about 20 on average in 2025, roughly 60-70 in Feb-Mar, and about 400 in April (around 20x last year's average), with about two-thirds attributed to a preview model. He says scanning is not the bottleneck.

key_ideas.idea: The harness is six steps: threat model and sandbox as per-codebase setup, then discovery, verification, triage and patch as the loop.
key_ideas.detail: Setup is a one-off investment per codebase. The loop runs on every scan. He frames the later steps as looking like a standard ML pipeline: recall, precision, ranking, closing the loop.

key_ideas.idea: A threat model is the missing system context: the model reads code well but not why the system was designed the way it was.
key_ideas.detail: Bootstrap a draft from docs, code comments, past patches and CVEs, then have the model interview experts for unwritten assumptions such as internal-only apps or compensating controls. The threat model is a document, and it doubles as context for triage. He reports true-positive rates around 90% with a well-documented threat model, and says above 75% is good.

key_ideas.idea: Sandboxes need isolation (no egress, no cloud credentials) and reproducibility (the same baseline container for every run).
key_ideas.detail: The example sandbox is three Docker images (app, Postgres, Redis), with the security agent outside the boundary probing over HTTP. One team called live testbeds where PoCs can be detonated the biggest lever.

key_ideas.idea: Discovery optimises recall and verification optimises precision, and they should be separate agents.
key_ideas.detail: If discovery verifies its own work in the loop, it may self-censor and lose recall. The verifier is independent: it sees only the vulnerability claim, not the discovery reasoning, and is told to assume the finding is false.

key_ideas.idea: Prompts should get simpler as models improve, and tools matter more than prompt detail.
key_ideas.detail: He cut his prompt size by about 50% with each new model generation. Asking the model to look for where untrusted data crosses a trust boundary works better than listing vulnerability classes. A pen-testing team that let the model call the API, read logs and read source reached nearly 100% true-positive rate because the model could verify inside the loop.

key_ideas.idea: Triage severity is impact times likelihood, and business context such as firewalls and internal-only exposure can change the rating a lot.
key_ideas.detail: The agent rated a SQL injection high. After human review, it was downgraded to low likelihood because of an application firewall and because the service is internal-only. That context must be written down (system design, docs, wiki) to reach the model.

key_ideas.idea: Close the loop: validate patches with a ladder and turn each fixed finding into a check so it cannot recur.
key_ideas.detail: Validation steps are: the original PoC stops working, the existing tests stay green, then a fresh discovery agent re-attacks the patch, with a human confirming before merge. Adding the scan as a regression check makes the harness improve with each run; he frames this as moving from operational expense to capital expense.

key_ideas.idea: Organisational bottlenecks (routing, severity calibration, patch bandwidth) appear once volume grows by orders of magnitude.
key_ideas.detail: At a dozen findings a month you can curate by hand, but at hundreds you need routing by code or service owner, which needs no LLM. Red and blue teams often disagree on what high severity means, so write the rules down once. Patching is the hardest part to automate, and he says he knows of few companies with fully automated patch review.

key_ideas.idea: Start small and interactive: open-source dependencies first, hands on the wheel, then automate once you know where the model fails.
key_ideas.detail: Learn where the model gets cut, what context it lacks and where precision is low before moving to automation. Scan, verify, triage and patch are all needed; scanning alone does not help.

techniques.name: Threat model as a living context document
techniques.how: Bootstrap from docs, code comments, past patches and CVEs; ask the model to infer unpatched CVEs; have the model interview domain experts for unwritten assumptions; feed the same document into discovery and triage.
techniques.when: Before any automated scan of a codebase, and when triage keeps mis-rating severity because business context is missing.

techniques.name: Isolated, reproducible PoC sandbox
techniques.how: Run the app with its real dependencies (e.g. Docker containers for app, Postgres, Redis) with no egress and no cloud credentials. Start every agent from the same pinned baseline container. The security agent sits outside the boundary and probes over HTTP.
techniques.when: When the agent must run untrusted code or deliberately detonate exploit proofs of concept to confirm true positives.

techniques.name: Independent adversarial verifier
techniques.how: Give a fresh agent only the vulnerability claim (no discovery traces) and instruct it to assume the claim is false. It builds a PoC and runs it in a fresh container. Confirm only if the exploit works.
techniques.when: After any discovery pass, to raise precision without suppressing recall in the discovery agent.

techniques.name: Tool-equipped discovery
techniques.how: Give the model tools to call the API, read responses and logs, and read source, so it can verify its hypotheses in the loop instead of only reading code.
techniques.when: When the model reads code and flags plausible issues that it cannot confirm.

techniques.name: Less prescriptive prompts for stronger models
techniques.how: Remove category checklists and write a short goal such as tracing where untrusted data hits a trust boundary. Cut prompt size each time the model is upgraded.
techniques.when: On each model upgrade, and when prescriptive prompts add noise or false positives.

techniques.name: Patch validation ladder with a generative verifier loop
techniques.how: Check that the original PoC fails after the patch, the test suite stays green, and a fresh discovery agent cannot re-attack the patch. Feed failures back to the patching agent. A human approves the merge.
techniques.when: Whenever an AI-generated security patch is proposed.

techniques.name: Close the loop as a regression check
techniques.how: Convert each confirmed and fixed finding into a scan rule or test so the same issue is caught next time.
techniques.when: After each fix, so the harness improves with each run instead of restarting from zero.

techniques.name: Severity triage as impact times likelihood with compensating controls
techniques.how: Dedupe and cluster findings, then rate impact (ring 0 vs ring 1) and likelihood (how many steps an attacker needs). Downgrade for firewalls or internal-only exposure, and upgrade for sensitive data such as PII or health data. Keep a human in the loop.
techniques.when: When verified findings exceed what engineers can absorb and low-value true positives are eroding trust.

techniques.name: Code-owner routing without an LLM
techniques.how: Send each finding to the owning team or service owner via a rule, and create a ticket there. An LLM is not required.
techniques.when: Once findings reach hundreds per month and manual curation stops scaling.

numbers.claim: Mozilla security bug fixes per month: about 20 average in 2025, around 60-70 in Feb-Mar, about 400 in April (roughly 20x last year's average); about two-thirds attributed to a preview model (~271).
Open-source scan of more than 1,000 repos: 23,000 candidates, 6,200 rated high or critical, 1,600 reported to maintainers, about 100 patched upstream (at time of update).
A well-documented threat model reportedly raised true-positive rate to about 90%; speaker says above 75% is great.
Prompt size cut by about 50% with each new model version.
A pen-testing team that gave the model API, log and source tools reached an almost 100% true-positive rate.

hot_takes: Scanning is not the bottleneck; verification, triage, patching and organisational process are.
Non-technical problems are an order of magnitude harder than technical ones.
Harness loops are operational expense until you close them, at which point they become capital expense.
Prompts should get shorter with each model generation, not longer.

relevance.why: Crucible runs sandboxed code execution with exec-gate guardrails. The talk's sandbox-plus-independent-verifier pattern maps onto that, and the precision/recall split is a useful eval design.
relevance.action: Add a separate verifier agent to any Crucible-driven security or bug check that sees only the claimed finding (not the discovery trace), must reproduce it in a fresh sandbox, and is measured on precision separately from discovery recall.

relevance.why: ProsHarness has a plan, critique (Codex) and debate flow. The talk argues the critic should be independent and adversarial, not sharing the producer's reasoning trace.
relevance.action: Check the critique step: pass the critic only the artifact or claim, not the planner's reasoning, and instruct it to assume the claim is wrong. Compare its hit rate with the current setup.

relevance.why: The verifier-separation and sandboxed PoC pattern applies to any agent that generates claims it has to confirm.
relevance.action: Read the transcript's verification section (11:28-13:28) as prior art for building a claim-verifier step.
